bye: PortScope stopped. You can close this tab.
intro_title: What can the network see of this machine?
intro_body: PortScope lists every port your computer is listening on, which program opened it, and whether your router forwards it to the Internet through UPnP. Nothing leaves your network.
scanning_upnp: Enumerating sockets and asking the router for its UPnP port mappings…
scan_done: {n} listening ports analysed · {crit} high or critical
no_token: No valid session. Open the link printed in the terminal where PortScope is running (launch links work only once).
fw_note_on: Ports listening on the network may still be blocked by firewall rules. The score assumes some of them are.
fw_note_off: Every port listening on the network is reachable by any device on it. Turn the firewall on.
fw_note_partial: Some network profiles have the firewall off. Public networks (cafés, hotels) are the dangerous ones.
fw_note_unknown: Could not read the firewall state. On Linux, run `sudo ufw status` to check.
upnp_skipped: UPnP discovery was skipped for this scan.
upnp_none: No router answered UPnP requests. That usually means UPnP is disabled, which is the safer setting.
double_nat: The router's public IP is private or CGNAT: there is another NAT upstream, so mappings may not reach the Internet.
upnp_open_note: These ports were opened on the router automatically by programs on your network. Each one is reachable from the Internet.
upnp_on_note: UPnP is enabled but nothing is forwarded right now. Any program on your LAN, including malware, can open ports without asking.
exp_internet_hint: Forwarded by the router: reachable from the Internet
exp_network_hint: Listening on a network interface: reachable from your LAN unless the firewall blocks it
exp_local_hint: Bound to loopback: only programs on this computer can connect
unknown_proc: unknown (run as admin/root to see it)
unknown_why: Not in the PortScope database. Check which program owns it: if you do not recognise it, look it up before trusting it.
upnp_forward: Router {gw} forwards external port {ext} here via UPnP ("{desc}").
guide_lead_local: Three levels, from best to fastest: stop the program that listens, make it listen only on this PC, or block the port in the firewall.
guide_lead_remote: This port belongs to another device ({host}). The fix is on the router, or on that device.
guide_warn: Before closing a port, make sure nothing you rely on needs it. Every block command comes with its undo.
g_win_admin: Run these commands in PowerShell as Administrator (right-click Start > Terminal (Admin)).
g_identify_win: Shows the program and, if it is a Windows service, the service name you need below.
g_identify_linux: Shows the process and the systemd unit that started it.
g_stop_win: Replace SERVICE_NAME with the service name from step 1. If it is a regular app, uninstall it or turn off its sharing/remote feature.
g_stop_core: Do not stop this one: it is a core Windows component and the system will break. Block the port in the firewall instead and turn off the related feature (sharing, Remote Desktop) if you do not use it.
g_stop_linux: Replace UNIT_NAME with the unit shown in step 1.
g_bind: Keep it, but only for this PC
g_bind_text: If you need the service locally, change its config to listen on 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0. It disappears from the network and stays usable here.
g_block_win: Creates an inbound block rule. Block rules win over allow rules in Windows Firewall.
g_verify_text: Run the scan again. The port should disappear or change to "This PC only".
tip_smb1: Disable SMBv1 (the protocol exploited by WannaCry). If you do not share folders or printers, you can also remove the shares listed.
tip_netbios: Disable NetBIOS over TCP/IP on every adapter (value 2). Modern Windows networks do not need it.
tip_rdp: Turn off Remote Desktop. To keep it, allow it only through a VPN and require Network Level Authentication.
tip_llmnr: Disable LLMNR via the same policy key Group Policy uses ("Turn off multicast name resolution").
tip_ssdp: Stops the SSDP Discovery service. Network discovery of media devices will stop working.
tip_winrm: Stops Windows Remote Management. Only do this if you do not manage this PC remotely.
tip_do: Settings > Windows Update > Advanced options > Delivery Optimization: turn off "Allow downloads from other PCs" or limit it to your local network.
tip_ssh: Check that both values are "no". If not, set PasswordAuthentication no and PermitRootLogin no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config and restart ssh.
tip_rpcbind: Only needed for NFS servers. Disable both the service and the socket.
tip_docker: Find where -H tcp://0.0.0.0:2375 is set and remove it. Use `docker context` over SSH for remote access.
tip_mysql: Set bind-address = 127.0.0.1 in the [mysqld] section and restart MySQL.
tip_pg: Set listen_addresses = 'localhost' in postgresql.conf and restart PostgreSQL.
tip_redis: Set bind 127.0.0.1 -::1, protected-mode yes and a requirepass in redis.conf.
tip_mongo: Set net.bindIp: 127.0.0.1 and security.authorization: enabled in mongod.conf.
r_model_unknown: The model is printed on the label under the router, and usually on the login page of its admin panel.
r_manual: Search the manufacturer's website for "{model} manual" or "{model} disable UPnP". Avoid third-party download sites.
r_open: Open the router admin page: http://{ip}
r_login: Log in with the admin password (label on the router if you never changed it, and change it if so).
r_find: Look for a section called UPnP, NAT, Port forwarding or Advanced > Network.
r_forward: If you created a manual port-forwarding rule for port {port}, delete it.
r_disable: Unless a game console or app truly needs it, turn UPnP off: programs (and malware) will no longer open ports on their own.
r_save: Save and apply. Some routers need a reboot.
r_verify: Run PortScope again: the mapping should be gone. If the router stops answering UPnP, the Router panel will say so.
bad_finding: This finding contains unexpected data, so no commands are shown. Re-run the scan.
